The Tanabe-Sugano tools available only support d²–d⁸ configurations. **d⁹ (Cu(II)) is not supported**, and this is actually expected for fundamental reasons:

## Why d⁹ Cannot Be Analyzed with Tanabe-Sugano Formalism

For d⁹ Cu(II), the electronic structure is fundamentally different from d²–d⁸:

1. **d⁹ is a one-hole system** (equivalent to d¹ but with inverted orbital energies)
2. **Only one spin-allowed d-d transition manifold exists** in octahedral symmetry
3. **The Racah parameter B does not affect spin-allowed transition energies** for d¹/d⁹ because there is no electron-electron repulsion splitting within the spin-allowed manifold (only one unpaired electron)

## Analysis of the Observed Spectrum

The complex shows tetragonal distortion (Jahn-Teller active d⁹ with axial water ligands), giving:

| Feature | Energy (cm⁻¹) | Assignment |
|---------|---------------|------------|
| Shoulder | ~12,240 | ²B₁g → ²A₁g (dₓ²₋ᵧ² → d₂²) |
| Main band | ~14,720 | ²B₁g → ²B₂g/²Eg (dₓ²₋ᵧ² → dₓᵧ/dₓ₂,dᵧ₂) |

For tetragonally distorted d⁹, the **average** of the transitions approximates 10Dq:

$$10Dq \approx \frac{12240 + 14720}{2} \approx 13,480 \text{ cm}^{-1}$$

$$Dq \approx 1,350 \text{ cm}^{-1}$$

However, **B cannot be determined** from d-d spectra for d⁹ systems—the spin-allowed transitions are independent of B. B can only be estimated from charge-transfer bands or by comparison to free-ion values (typically B ≈ 800–1000 cm⁻¹ for Cu(II) complexes, showing nephelauxetic reduction from the free-ion value of ~1200 cm⁻¹).
